Description: Philistine bichrome pottery is the red-and-black painted ware of the early Philistines, decorated with spirals, metopes, triglyphs, birds, and geometric panels on a white slip. It followed the locally made Mycenaean IIIC monochrome ware (Philistine 1) of the 12th century BC and dominated at Tel Miqne-Ekron and the other Philistine cities during the 11th century BC, before fading as Philistine culture assimilated into local Canaanite styles. The ware is found at all five Philistine cities - Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath, and Gaza - and marks the arrival of the Aegean Sea Peoples whom the Bible calls Philistines.
HistoricalPeriod: Iron Age I, c. 12th-11th centuries BC
Interpretations: Bichrome pottery is the archaeologist's fingerprint for the Philistines: where it appears, the Sea Peoples settled, giving a material map of the Philistine pentapolis behind the stories of Samson, Saul, and David. It is a ware type, not a single object, so it has no single discovery date or museum home - and it proves Philistine presence, not any individual biblical episode. Its Aegean style also confirms the Bible's own account that the Philistines came from across the sea (Amos 9:7 speaks of Caphtor).
RelatedEvents: David and Goliath; Samson and Delilah
BiblicalSignificance: Bichrome ware lets readers see the Philistines of Judges and Samuel as a real, datable people with a distinctive Aegean culture on the coastal plain - not a literary invention.
DiscoveryLocation: Philistine cities: Ashdod; Ashkelon; Ekron (Tel Miqne); Gath; Gaza
